introduction: These hundred readings return to the life of Jesus as a pattern: awaited for centuries, he came without rank or army, was opposed by the learned and powerful of his day, was mocked, crowned with thorns and put to death, forgave those who did it, and was honoured across the world only long afterwards. Many are notes of talks, and they speak throughout of the Jews as those who rejected him; the same pattern is then traced in the reception of Muhammad and of Bahá’u’lláh. The Gospel passages on which the readings draw are set beside them. So are passages that keep the telling fair: the Jews in the Gospels who did recognize him, Nicodemus and Gamaliel among the Pharisees, Paul's warning not to boast against the branches, the Council's rejection of collective blame, Maimonides on how prophecy is read, and Dostoevsky's reminder that a church may turn its own Lord away.
questions: The readings say that those who were waiting most eagerly failed to recognize the one they waited for. What in a person's expectations can hide from them the thing expected?
Simeon, Nicodemus, Joseph of Arimathea, the Bereans and three thousand in Jerusalem were Jews who responded. How should that change the way the story of rejection is told?
The Second Vatican Council taught that the passion cannot be charged against all Jews. Why does that correction matter, and what harm has the opposite teaching done?
Dostoevsky imagines the church itself sending Christ away. In what ways might the followers of any religion repeat what the readings describe?
Jesus forgave from the cross and Stephen under the stones. What makes forgiveness of that kind possible, and what is it for?
The powerful of that age are forgotten and a man they ignored is remembered. What does that suggest about how to judge what matters in your own time?

outside.why: Isaiah speaks of one despised and rejected of men, a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief.
Jesus told his disciples that the Son of man must suffer many things, and be rejected, and be slain.
These are the words from the cross as Luke gives them: Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do.
Stephen, the first to die for his faith in Jesus, cried as he was stoned: Lord, lay not this sin to their charge.
John's Gospel says: he came unto his own, and his own received him not.
Paul reminds the Corinthians that not many wise, not many mighty, not many noble are called.
Mark's Gospel notes in passing that the common people heard him gladly.
Nicodemus, a Pharisee and a ruler, came to Jesus by night and called him a teacher come from God. What does his visit say about speaking of the Pharisees as a single body of opponents?
Luke tells of Simeon in Jerusalem, a just and devout man waiting for the consolation of Israel, who recognized the child.
The Book of Acts praises the Jews of Berea, who received the word with readiness and searched the scriptures daily whether those things were so.

The Second Vatican Council declared that what happened in the passion of Christ cannot be charged against all the Jews then alive, nor against the Jews of today. How should a reader keep that in mind where these talks say that the Jews rejected him?
Jesus told a Samaritan woman: salvation is of the Jews. What do those who honour Jesus owe to the people and the scripture he came from?
Luke tells of Joseph, a counsellor and a good man who had not consented to the deed, who went to Pilate and begged the body of Jesus.
Acts records that the number of the disciples multiplied in Jerusalem, and a great company of the priests were obedient to the faith.
The Pharisees in John's Gospel ask their officers: have any of the rulers or of the Pharisees believed on him?
Jesus thanked the Father for hiding these things from the wise and prudent and revealing them unto babes.
Habakkuk is told of the vision: though it tarry, wait for it; because it will surely come.
Two disciples on the road said sadly: we trusted that it had been he which should have redeemed Israel.
Moses foretold a prophet into whose mouth God would put His words.
Paul, an Israelite, asks whether God has cast away His people, and answers: God forbid. How does his answer bear on the way the story of rejection is told?
The Qur’an has the believers say: we make no distinction between any of His messengers.
The Letter to the Hebrews says that the God who spoke in time past by the prophets has in these last days spoken by a Son.
Jesus said: think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets; I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil.
Moses commanded: ye shall not add unto the word which I command you. What would loyalty to that command have looked like to a devout hearer of a new teacher?
Jesus charged some teachers with laying aside the commandment of God to hold the tradition of men.
Nicodemus asked his fellow Pharisees: doth our law judge any man, before it hear him, and know what he doeth?
Jesus answered the charge of sabbath-breaking: the sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath.
The risen Jesus says to two of his own followers: O fools, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken.
Paul speaks of a vail upon the heart when the old writings are read.
William Blake wrote of two readers of the same book: both read the Bible day and night, but thou read'st black where I read white. What makes two sincere readers find opposite things in one text?
Isaiah foretells that the wolf shall dwell with the lamb, and a little child shall lead them.

Maimonides, the great rabbi of the twelfth century, wrote that Isaiah's wolf and lamb are a metaphor and a parable. What does his reading show about the claim that Jewish expectation was simply literal?
In John's Gospel some said, this is the Christ, and others asked: shall Christ come out of Galilee?
When Jesus healed a man, the people were amazed, and some said it was done by the prince of devils.
Asked by Pilate whether he was a king, Jesus answered: my kingdom is not of this world.
Zechariah foretells a king who comes lowly, and riding upon an ass.
Jesus said to those who asked a sign: ye can discern the face of the sky, but can ye not discern the signs of the times?
Maimonides taught that one should not presume the Messianic king must work miracles and wonders. By what, then, would a careful community recognize the one it awaits?
Paul says that a crucified Christ was unto the Jews a stumblingblock, and unto the Greeks foolishness.
The council saw that Peter and John were unlearned men, and took knowledge of them that they had been with Jesus.
Paul says that knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth, and that whoever thinks he knows anything knows nothing yet as he ought.
Jesus called certain teachers blind leaders of the blind, and said that both shall fall into the ditch.
Jesus said to two fishermen: follow me, and I will make you fishers of men.
The people of his own town asked: is not this the carpenter? And they were offended at him.

The Pharisee Gamaliel advised the council to let the apostles alone: if this work be of men it will come to nought, but if it be of God ye cannot overthrow it. What does his counsel add to the picture of how the learned responded?
Paul says that God has chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty.
The Roman historian Tacitus records of the first Christians put to death in Rome that mockery of every sort was added to their deaths.
The Qur’an says: never came there unto them a messenger but they did mock him.
Jesus said: the foxes have holes, and the birds of the air have nests, but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head.
Paul says that he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.
Luke says that the risen Jesus opened his disciples' understanding, that they might understand the scriptures.
Matthew tells how the governor's soldiers put on him a scarlet robe and a crown of thorns, and bowed the knee in mockery.
Isaiah says: he was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth.
The first letter of Peter says that when he was reviled, he reviled not again; when he suffered, he threatened not.
Jesus taught: love your enemies, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you.
Jesus said to Peter: the cup which my Father hath given me, shall I not drink it?
The Letter to the Hebrews says that for the joy set before him he endured the cross, despising the shame.

The Qur’an says of those who claimed to have killed the Messiah: they slew him not nor crucified him, but it appeared so unto them. How do you weigh the difference between this account and the Gospels', and what do the two agree on?
The Qur’an says: We gave unto Jesus, son of Mary, clear proofs, and We supported him with the Holy Spirit.
As he came near Jerusalem Jesus beheld the city and wept over it.
The psalm says that the stone which the builders refused is become the head stone of the corner.
Jesus likened the kingdom of heaven to leaven hid in three measures of meal, till the whole was leavened.
Acts says that on the day of Pentecost about three thousand souls in Jerusalem gladly received the word.
Zechariah hears: not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit.
Jesus told his disciples: if they have persecuted me, they will also persecute you.
Shakespeare gives Shylock, mocked and spat upon in a Christian city, the words: hath not a Jew eyes? What happened in later centuries when those who had been persecuted held power over others?
Gibbon describes how a pure and humble religion grew up in silence and obscurity and derived new vigour from opposition.

In Dostoevsky's story the Grand Inquisitor, a prince of the church, says to the returned Christ: why hast Thou come to hinder us? Is the rejection of a Messenger something one people did once, or something any established religion may do?
Emerson said that churches are not built on the principles of Jesus but on his tropes. Who, in the long history of his Cause, has understood him?
Tertullian told the persecutors of his day: the oftener we are mown down by you, the more in number we grow.
Paul says that he made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant.
Luke begins his Gospel by saying that many have taken in hand to set forth what eyewitnesses delivered.
Isaiah says: surely he hath borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows; yet we did esteem him stricken.
Isaiah says that the people that walked in darkness have seen a great light.
Jesus said that a corn of wheat, if it die, bringeth forth much fruit.
Shelley imagined the ruined statue of a king of kings, of whose works nothing beside remains. What does it mean that the powerful of that age are forgotten and a man they ignored is not?
Jesus lamented: O Jerusalem, how often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens.
Jesus said: woe unto you, when all men shall speak well of you. Which says more about a teacher: the contempt of his own day or the honour of later centuries?
By the lake the risen Jesus asked Peter three times: lovest thou me?
The people were astonished, for he taught them as one having authority, and not as the scribes.
Moses himself said of the people he had led out of Egypt: I am not able to bear all this people alone, because it is too heavy for me.
The Qur’an tells its Prophet: messengers indeed have been denied before thee, and they were patient under the denial.
In the Qur’an the messenger says: O my Lord, mine own folk make this Qur’an of no account.
Thomas Carlyle, in his lectures on heroes, called Muhammad a silent great soul, one of those who cannot but be in earnest.
The Chronicles say that God sent messengers because He had compassion on His people, but they mocked the messengers of God.
Stephen asked his judges: which of the prophets have not your fathers persecuted?
The Qur’an says that the nearest in affection to the believers are those who say: we are Christians.
In the Qur’an the angels announce to Mary a word from God, whose name is the Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary.

In Boccaccio's tale a Jew tells a sultan that each of the three peoples deems itself to have the true law, and that the question remains pendent. What moves the followers of one religion to speak well of another?
William Penn wrote that the humble, meek, merciful and just souls are everywhere of one religion.
This is the verse the reading recalls: the Jews say, God's hand is fettered; nay, but both His hands are spread out wide in bounty.
Isaiah had said the same to his own people: behold, the Lord's hand is not shortened, that it cannot save.
Amos warned those who longed for the day of the Lord: to what end is it for you? The day of the Lord is darkness, and not light.
Jesus warned that false Christs and false prophets would arise and show great signs. How is a community to be both watchful against false claims and open to a true one?
Jesus said: a prophet is not without honour, save in his own country, and in his own house.
Through Amos God says to Israel: you only have I known of all the families of the earth; therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities.
Paul warns Gentile Christians, grafted like a wild olive into the tree: boast not against the branches. What would he say to anyone who tells the story of Israel's unbelief with satisfaction?
Deuteronomy says that the nations will hear the statutes and say: surely this great nation is a wise and understanding people.
Micah says that all people will walk every one in the name of his god, and we will walk in the name of the Lord our God for ever. What is to be honoured in a people's faithfulness to its own law?
The Qur’an bids its Prophet say: O People of the Scripture, come to an agreement between us and you.

isaiah-despised-and-rejected.text: He is despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief: and we hid as it were our faces from him; he was despised, and we esteemed him not

luke-wept-over-the-city.text: And when he was come near, he beheld the city, and wept over it, Saying, If thou hadst known, even thou, at least in this thy day, the things which belong unto thy peace! but now they are hid from thine eyes

john-have-any-of-the-rulers-believed.text: Then answered them the Pharisees, Are ye also deceived? Have any of the rulers or of the Pharisees believed on him? But this people who knoweth not the law are cursed

hebrews-endured-the-cross.text: Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith; who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is set down at the right hand of the throne of God

luke-joseph-of-arimathaea.text: And, behold, there was a man named Joseph, a counsellor; and he was a good man, and a just: (The same had not consented to the counsel and deed of them;) he was of Arimathaea, a city of the Jews: who also himself waited for the kingdom of God. This man went unto Pilate, and begged the body of Jesus

acts-company-of-the-priests.text: And the word of God increased; and the number of the disciples multiplied in Jerusalem greatly; and a great company of the priests were obedient to the faith

luke-son-of-man-must-suffer.text: The Son of man must suffer many things, and be rejected of the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be slain, and be raised the third day

mark-common-people-heard-him-gladly.text: And the common people heard him gladly

acts-three-thousand-souls.text: Then they that gladly received his word were baptized: and the same day there were added unto them about three thousand souls

philippians-obedient-unto-death.text: And being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross

quran-they-slew-him-not.text: And because of their saying: We slew the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, Allah's messenger - they slew him not nor crucified him, but it appeared so unto them; and lo! those who disagree concerning it are in doubt thereof; they have no knowledge thereof save pursuit of a conjecture; they slew him not for certain.
